flashcard_questions.a: Making one product at a time, crafted to the customer's exact specifications.
Making a set number of identical products together as a group.
Using assembly lines to mass-produce identical products in a continuous process.
Requiring large investment in machinery and technology rather than human labour.
Supplies are delivered exactly when needed for production, cutting warehousing costs.
How effectively a business converts its inputs into outputs.

flashcard_questions.q: What makes a service different from a good?
flashcard_questions.a: It is intangible, so it cannot be touched.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are workers well motivated under job production?
flashcard_questions.a: They see a product through from start to finish.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are unit costs high in job production?
What flexibility advantage does batch production have over flow production?
flashcard_questions.a: The business can switch between products to respond to changing demand.

flashcard_questions.q: What is idle time in batch production?
flashcard_questions.a: The wasted time between batches while machines are reconfigured.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is flow production described as inflexible?
flashcard_questions.a: Changing the production line to make different products is difficult and expensive.

flashcard_questions.q: Which electric car does Tesla mass-produce on a flow production line?
Which sportswear company uses batch production for different shoe designs and colourways?
How much can a handmade Fender guitar sell for?

notes: 15 cards: 7 term→definition (job, batch, flow, capital-intensive, JIT, productivity, service), 5 single-fact advantage/disadvantage cards split one per fact (job motivation, job unit costs, batch flexibility, idle time, flow inflexibility), 3 concept→named example (Tesla Model 3, Nike, Fender £10,000). No formula or calculation content in this lesson, so those card types are not used.
